body:
TIL you can't do the following cast in C, but you can in C++ char ** x = /* … */;
const char * const * y = x;

comments.notes:
The reason it fails in C being that the following cast is not allowed in either C nor C++, and C wanted to have less complicated logic: char ** x = /* … */;
const char **y = x;
*y = “yahoo!”; // allowed because *y is not const qualified (only **y is)
x[0] += 1; // bad! yahoo is likely stored in the text section of the program (read only)!
I found this when I was reading through https://c-faq.com/

body: TIL if you malloc() something large enough, the kernel can decide to instead give you some random non-heap memory just wherever.

comments.notes: Balancing memory fragmentation with fast allocation is tricky. Contrary my original belief, you are not simply given an increasing address in the heap. On Linux there are 3 main layers that malloc is an interface to. The first is your c library's allocator, the second is the syscall `sblk()`, and the third is the syscall `mmap()`. Of course, this is a deep rabbit hole (I have not delved into), but put simply: (1) glibc is pre-allocated with a fixed allocator that is great for small allocations. (2) sblk represents the heap we think of; allocations are simple increases to the shared heap address. But make sure you deallocate soon, or you'll block the heap from being able to reclaim memory. (3) mmap is the mother of all memory syscalls, and good for large allocations. You can grab an arbitrary segment of virtual address space, then blocks get paged into physical memory as you go. In a 64-bit address space, this fixes all problems with fragmentation at the cost of expensive bookkeeping.
